transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2028-03-08
Start: 10:00am PT
Duration: ~45 minutes
Attendees: Alyssa Chen (Redwood AE), Raj Patel (Redwood SE), Marta Lopez (HarborTrust, Head of ML), Ethan Cole (HarborTrust, Eng Mgr), Priya Singh (HarborTrust, Security)

[00:00:00] Alyssa: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, quick check in — how's the week been on your side?
[00:00:10] Marta: Hi Alyssa, pretty busy, but we ran the streaming test you sent, got some odd TTFT spikes at higher concurrencies.
[00:00:22] Raj: thanks, can you say what config — streaming enabled, model variant, sequence length?
[00:00:28] Marta: streaming on, model is rwd-7b-v2-quant, sequence around 1.2k median but tail near 6k, concurrency 16 in our pilot.
[00:00:40] Raj: OK that explains some KV cache behavior; with 6k tails we see kernel thrash if the runtime picks small attention kernels. We tried an alternate kernel selector that keeps large sequence kernels for tails.
[00:00:55] Ethan: we're seeing TTFT ranges 120ms median but 450ms 95th, sometimes >800ms on spikes — that's the problem for our latency SLOs.
[00:01:08] Raj: median 120ms is decent, but TTFT spikes often from batching and compilation pauses or fallback to non-optimized kernels; did you see any compilation logs?
[00:01:18] Marta: some logs show 'fallback to generic kernel' messages, not sure why.
[00:01:25] Alyssa: likely kernel mismatch at runtime; Raj, can you summarize what we looked at last week?
[00:01:30] Raj: sure — last week we saw that with sequence skew (many short, some long), the runtime's automatic kernel selector sometimes chooses a faster small-seq kernel that can't handle the occasional 6k sequence, causing a fallback path. For streaming, TTFT also depends on the first chunk size and how we flush the prefix.
[00:01:50] Ethan: if we reduce initial chunk to 64 tokens — does that help TTFT?
[00:01:56] Raj: it can lower time to first token but may increase overall token count and slightly raise cost. The balance depends on your SLOs; since HarborTrust cares about first token for UX, we can tune chunk size to 32 or 64 and test.
[00:02:12] Priya: also security — do any of the performance changes impact KMS or audit log flow? We need to ensure encryption in transit doesn't add jitter.
[00:02:22] Alyssa: good point, we ensure KMS calls occur asynchronously and don't block the inference path. Our Private deployment keeps keys customer-managed; we can show instrumentation.
[00:02:33] Marta: can you walk through kernel options again — you mentioned Triton kernels vs Redwood custom kernels?
[00:02:40] Raj: Yes — Triton tends to be great for medium seq lengths and batched workloads; our custom kernels are optimized for long sequences and reduced memory copies. For quantized models, kernel choice matters more; some Triton kernels don't yet exploit int8 perf as well as our custom path.
[00:02:58] Marta: interesting. In our sample, the quantized 7b model had lower median but worse tail.
[00:03:05] Raj: that's consistent — quantization reduces compute but can increase variance when kernels are not perfectly matched to sequence length. Also compilation/just-in-time kernel selection can add jitter.
[00:03:18] Ethan: what's your recommendation for our next run — streaming on or off?
[00:03:23] Raj: recommendation: run two experiments in parallel — streaming with small initial chunk (32 tokens) and non-streaming with server-side buffering that returns at 150ms target. Collect TTFT, p50/p95/p99, and CPU/GPU utilization traces.
[00:03:38] Alyssa: we'll provide an updated runbook template — Raj will produce the kernel config matrix to test.
[00:03:44] Marta: timeline? we need results before our product review next week.
[00:03:48] Alyssa: we can prioritize — initial results by Friday.

[00:20:02] Raj: jumping ahead — I ran a quick internal sim yesterday: keeping a short-first-chunk reduced TTFT median by ~30% but P99 still depends on long-seq handling; switching to our large-seq kernel cut P99 by ~40% in that sim.
[00:20:16] Ethan: do you have numbers for concurrency 16 and 32?
[00:20:20] Raj: yes: at concurrency 16 median 110ms p99 680ms with Triton, with custom kernel median 90ms p99 410ms. At 32, Triton p99 >1s, custom kernel ~620ms.
[00:20:34] Marta: that's promising. Any cost delta?
[00:20:37] Raj: marginal — custom kernel reduces GPU time per token so cost slightly down; but if you run more reserved capacity to hit SLOs, committed cost rises. We'll include cost-per-1000-token estimates.
[00:20:48] Priya: on auditing: can we see trace IDs from the infra so we can tie high-latency requests to customer logs?
[00:20:55] Alyssa: yes, we surface trace IDs and request metadata in the Console and can push to your SIEM via webhook.

[00:31:10] Marta: about sequence length distribution — attaching our histogram would help; current median 1.2k, 90th 3.8k, 99th 6.4k.
[00:31:22] Raj: perfect — that helps pick kernel thresholds. Also consider prefix caching for repeated prompts — if you have common prefixes we can cache KV to reduce compute and TTFT.
[00:31:33] Ethan: we do have a set of standard customer prompts — can Redwood cache those?
[00:31:37] Raj: yes, prefix/KV caching is supported; caching reduces TTFT for repeated prefixes a lot. We'll instrument hit rates in the runbook.

[00:38:05] Priya: security quick question — private deployment with customer-managed KMS, does Redwood still keep access logs?
[00:38:12] Alyssa: we keep audit logs but you control key material; logs can be shipped to your SIEM and we've got SOC2 docs coming.
[00:38:20] Priya: ok please send sample audit format.

[00:40:00] Alyssa: Recap — action items: Raj to run kernel comparisons and share CSV; Marta to send histograms and sample traces; Alyssa to send security docs and updated runbook. We'll aim to deliver initial benchmark results by 2028-03-10 and schedule infra deep-dive 2028-03-14.
[00:40:20] Ethan: sounds good, thanks everyone.
[00:40:25] Marta: thanks, talk soon.
[00:40:30] Alyssa: thanks all, bye.

End of transcript
